title: Posterior Drawer Test | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Tear Assessment
structure: Posterior cruciate ligament; posterior tibial translation at 90° flexion.
procedure: Patient supine, hip 45° and knee 90° flexion; the examiner may sit on the forefoot. Palpate the joint line with the thumbs, grasp the tibia from anterior and translate it posteriorly in an explosive movement.
positive: Soft or mushy end-feel, or increased posterior translation compared with the other knee.
notes: Page: very accurate to confirm and rule out PCL tears. Other PCL tests: posterior sag sign/Godfrey/step-off, quadriceps active test, reverse Lachman.

title: Posterior Sag Sign | Godfrey's Test | Step-Off Test
purpose: Assess posterior cruciate ligament integrity by observing posterior sag of the tibia.
structure: Posterior cruciate ligament. PCL tears are often undiagnosed; typical mechanisms are dashboard trauma, a fall on the anterior proximal tibia with a flexed knee, or hyperextension.
procedure: Patient supine, hips 45° and knees 90° flexion, quadriceps fully relaxed; view the knee from the side. Progression (Godfrey's sign): hips and knees at 90° with the heels supported by the examiner, so gravity accentuates the sag.
positive: Loss of the normal step in which the tibia sits about 1 cm anterior to the femur (step-off), or visible posterior sag.

accuracy.source: Rubinstein et al. 1994 (only study reporting specificity)

notes: Good clinical value to confirm PCL tears. Other PCL tests: posterior drawer, quadriceps active test, reverse Lachman.

title: Quadriceps Active Test | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Tear Assessment
purpose: Detect PCL tears by letting the quadriceps pull a posteriorly sagging tibia back into position.
structure: Posterior cruciate ligament; quadriceps force vector, which includes an anterior-drawer component only when the knee is flexed beyond the quadriceps neutral angle (about 60-70°).
procedure: Patient supine, hip 45°, knee 90°, feet flat, neutral rotation. The examiner fixates the foot by gently sitting on it and asks the patient to slide the foot forward against resistance. Optional second part: isometric hamstring contraction to accentuate the posterior sag.
positive: The posteriorly sagged tibia shifts forward with quadriceps contraction. Forward shift without a prior posterior sag may indicate an ACL tear instead.

accuracy.source: Rubinstein et al. 1994 (most specific PCL test in that study; only one other study has evaluated it)

notes: Good clinical value to confirm a PCL tear. Other PCL tests: posterior drawer, posterior sag sign, reverse Lachman.

title: Reverse Lachman Test | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Tear Assessment
purpose: Assess PCL integrity at 30° flexion when the posterior drawer test is too uncomfortable in the acutely injured knee.
structure: Posterior cruciate ligament (maximal resistance to posterior translation at 90°); posterolateral corner if translation increases at 30° but not at 90°.
procedure: Patient supine, knee 30° flexion (stabilize with your knee underneath). Contralateral hand on the femur from lateral, ipsilateral hand on the tibia from medial, both close to the joint line to translate rather than angulate. The tibia must be anatomically reduced at the start, rotation neutral. Apply a posteriorly directed force to the tibia and judge end-feel and translation.
positive: Soft or absent end-feel with increased posterior translation compared with the other side. Grading (Lubowitz et al. 2008): grade 1 = 0-5 mm, plateau stays anterior to the condyle; grade 2 = 6-10 mm, plateau flush; grade 3 = >10 mm, plateau posterior to the condyle.

accuracy.source: Rubinstein et al. 1994 (only validity study found)

notes: Moderate clinical value to confirm a PCL tear. Increased translation on reverse Lachman but not on posterior drawer suggests a posterolateral corner injury; use the dial test to differentiate. SOURCE NOTE: the page's header section is titled 'Valgus Stress Test for MCL Injuries' in the API (copy error); the body is about the reverse Lachman test.

title: Dial Test / Loomer Test | Posterolateral Rotatory Instability of the Knee
purpose: Diagnose posterolateral corner (PLC) injuries and distinguish them from PCL tears.
structure: Posterolateral corner: lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament are the key stabilizers. PLC injuries follow blows to the anteromedial knee, hyperextension or non-contact varus stress and usually accompany ACL/PCL tears (only 28% isolated).
procedure: Original version prone (also possible supine or sitting). Knees flexed 30°, ankles in maximal dorsiflexion to limit ankle rotation; cup both heels with fingers along the talocalcaneal contours, maximally externally rotate both heels and measure the foot-thigh angle side to side. Repeat at 90° knee flexion.
positive: Side difference ≥ 10° of external rotation. Increased rotation at 30° but not at 90° = isolated PLC injury (an intact PCL restrains rotation at 90°); increased at both 30° and 90° = PLC plus PCL injury.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Krause et al. 2013, intra-tester 0.83-0.89, inter-tester 0.74-0.83 in healthy persons with a handheld inclinometer; validity unknown

notes: Page makes no recommendation on clinical utility because validity is unknown. Other PLC tests: reverse pivot shift, frog leg.

title: Reverse Pivot-Shift Test | Posterolateral Rotatory Instability Assessment
purpose: Assess posterolateral rotatory instability; evaluated so far only for PCL tears.
structure: Posterolateral corner (LCL, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament); lateral tibial plateau subluxes posteriorly in flexion and is reduced by the iliotibial band at about 30°.
procedure: Patient supine, knee 90° flexion. Ipsilateral hand externally rotates the tibia; contralateral hand on the proximal lateral tibia applies valgus while an axial load is applied through the tibia with the forearm or iliac crest. Passively extend the knee while maintaining external rotation, valgus and axial load.
positive: A clunk as the tibia reduces at about 30° flexion (the iliotibial band switches from a flexion to an extension vector). Apprehension in the awake patient can also be taken as positive.

accuracy.source: Rubinstein et al. 1994; no study has evaluated it for PLC lesions

notes: Moderate clinical value to confirm PCL tears, not useful to rule them out. Other PLC tests: dial/Loomer, frog leg.

title: Frog Leg Test | Posterolateral Rotatory Instability | PLC Assessment
purpose: Assess posterolateral knee instability (Gomes et al. 2016) by comparing lateral compartment gapping under varus in a frog-leg position.
structure: Lateral collateral ligament, lateral joint line and posterolateral corner. PLC injuries are rarely isolated and can follow failed ACL reconstruction.
procedure: Patient supine, both knees flexed 90° with the soles touching (frog position). Place the hypothenar of each hand on the anteromedial tibia, middle fingers palpating the LCL, joint line and PLC, and apply varus to both knees simultaneously.
positive: Noticeably greater palpable lateral gapping on the affected side than on the unaffected side.

accuracy.source: Gomes et al. 2016 (vs varus stress test and MRI; inter-rater kappa 0.86); not yet confirmed by other studies

notes: Page rates moderate clinical value for now. Norris & McNicholas 2017 (letter) argue the position loads the LCL but, with the femur externally rotated and the tibia relatively internally rotated, cannot properly stress the popliteus/popliteofibular structures, so PLC injuries without LCL involvement may be missed. Other PLC tests: dial, reverse pivot shift.

title: Valgus Stress Test for Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
purpose: Assess medial collateral ligament (MCL) integrity, one of the most prevalent knee injuries in primary care.
structure: Medial collateral ligament and medial joint line.
procedure: At 0°: hold the knee in full extension, secure the ankle with one hand, other hand around the knee with the thenar against the fibular head; push the knee medially and the ankle laterally to open the medial joint, palpating the medial joint line for gapping and pain. At 30°: same, with the knee on a cushion or the examiner's thigh.
positive: Pain and/or laxity (medial gapping) at 30° flexion.

accuracy.source: Kastelein et al. 2008, valgus stress at 30°, stand-alone

notes: Absence of both pain and laxity is at least moderately useful to exclude MCL lesions; confirming them with this test alone is not possible with acceptable certainty (see MCL cluster). Companion: varus stress test for the LCL.

title: Varus Stress Test for Lateral Collateral Ligament Injuries
structure: Lateral collateral ligament and lateral joint line.
procedure: Patient supine, knee in 30° flexion (maximally loose-packed position) on a cushion or the edge of the bed so the patient can relax. Fixate the femur with one hand, add slight lateral rotation and passively adduct the knee to stress the LCL.
positive: Excessive lateral gapping and/or reproduction of the patient's pain.

accuracy.source: Harilainen 1987 (only study; rated poor accuracy, no specificity reported)

notes: Little is known about its validity. SOURCE NOTE: the page heading reads 'Valgus Stress Test for Lateral Collateral Ligament Injuries' although the test is the varus stress test (typo on source). Companion: valgus stress test for the MCL.

title: MCL Cluster | Diagnosing Medial Collateral Ligament Injuries
purpose: Clinical prediction model (Kastelein et al. 2008) combining history and the valgus stress test to diagnose MCL lesions in general practice.
procedure: Of 36 candidate variables, four remained: history items (1) trauma by an external force to the leg, (2) rotational trauma; examination items (3) pain during the valgus stress test at 30°, (4) laxity during that test.
positive: At least 1 of the 2 history items AND pain on valgus stress at 30° → LR+ 4.8 for an MCL lesion; if laxity is also present → LR+ 6.4. Only one history item with no positive examination findings → MCL lesion can reasonably be excluded.
notes: Reduces unnecessary imaging referrals. Even when a lesion is suspected, guidelines recommend conservative management unless there is knee locking or suspected fracture.

title: McMurray Test for Meniscus Lesions
purpose: Detect meniscus tears, mainly of the posterior horns.
structure: Medial and lateral menisci (posterior aspect; the anterior half is less well loaded by this test).
procedure: Patient supine, knee fully flexed. Rotate the tibia medially and extend the knee, repeating at different flexion angles to cover the whole posterior lateral meniscus. For the medial meniscus, fully flex and rotate the tibia laterally, then extend.
positive: Clicking, locking or pain in the knee.

accuracy.source: Smith et al. 2015 meta-analysis; Blyth et al. 2015 found overall diagnostic accuracy of 63% in clinicians' hands

notes: Moderately useful to confirm, weak to rule out a meniscus tear. Other meniscus tests: Apley, Thessaly, joint line tenderness, Ege's, duck walk, Finochietto, bounce home.

title: Thessaly Test | Meniscus Tear Assessment
purpose: Weight-bearing provocation test for meniscus lesions.
structure: Medial and lateral menisci under load and rotation.
procedure: Test the uninjured leg first. The patient stands on the injured leg with the knee flexed 20°, holding the examiner's arms for support, and rotates the body over the tibia three times to each side.

accuracy.source: Goossens et al. 2015 (higher-quality study vs arthroscopy); Karachalios et al. 2005 originally described it as the most accurate meniscus test

notes: Not an accurate test, but Apley's and McMurray do not perform much better; consider MRI when history suggests a meniscus lesion. Other meniscus tests: McMurray, joint line tenderness, Ege's, Apley's, duck walk, Finochietto.

title: Apley's Test for Meniscus Tears
purpose: Differentiate meniscal from ligamentous lesions using rotation under compression versus distraction.
procedure: Patient prone, knee 90° flexion, tested thigh fixated with the examiner's leg. Rotate the tibia laterally and medially under distraction (look for excessive rotation or discomfort), then repeat under compression (look for decreased rotation or discomfort).
positive: Rotation plus distraction more painful or more mobile than the other side → probably ligamentous; rotation plus compression more painful or less mobile → probably meniscus damage.

accuracy.source: Hegedus et al. 2007 meta-analysis; Blyth et al. 2015 overall accuracy 58%

notes: Weak accuracy to confirm or rule out meniscus tears. Other meniscus tests: McMurray, Thessaly, joint line tenderness, Ege's, duck walk, Finochietto, bounce home.

title: Ege's Test / Weight-bearing McMurray's Test | Meniscus Tear Assessment
purpose: Weight-bearing version of the McMurray test for meniscus tears, since most meniscal symptoms occur in weight bearing.
structure: Medial meniscus (squat in external rotation) and lateral meniscus (squat in internal rotation).
procedure: Patient stands with knees extended and feet 30-40 cm apart. Medial meniscus: squat with both legs in maximal external rotation and slowly stand up (knees move apart and externally rotate). Lateral meniscus: squat and stand with both legs in maximal internal rotation, slightly less than a full squat, support allowed (knees move together). Stop as soon as pain or a click occurs.
positive: Pain and/or a click (sometimes audible) at the corresponding joint line, usually around 90° flexion; pain when rising from the squat also counts. Anterior tears provoke symptoms earlier in flexion, posterior-horn tears in deeper flexion.

accuracy.source: Akseki et al. 2004 (single well-conducted study; performed better than McMurray and joint line tenderness)

notes: Moderate clinical value. Not suitable in the very acute stage (needs pain-free weight bearing and squatting). Accuracy lower with degenerative arthritis or patellofemoral disease, higher in ACL-deficient knees and knees with effusion. Other meniscus tests: McMurray, joint line tenderness, duck walk, Apley's, Finochietto, Thessaly.

title: Joint Line Tenderness | Meniscus Tear Assessment
purpose: Palpation of the joint line for meniscus tears; per Smith et al. 2015 the best clinical tool available.
structure: Medial and lateral menisci at the tibiofemoral joint line. Prevalence on the page: 57% symptomatic / 36% asymptomatic (Switzerland), 32% / 23% (USA); 2 per 1000 new diagnoses per year in the Netherlands.
procedure: Patient supine, knee 90° flexion (makes the anterior menisci more palpable). Rotate the tibia internally so the femoral condyle pushes the medial meniscus forward, palpate along the medial joint line and watch the reaction; rotate externally and palpate the lateral joint line.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain.
notes: Page rates moderate clinical value. Other meniscus tests: McMurray, Finochietto, Ege's, Apley's, duck walk, Thessaly.

title: Duck Walk Test / Childress Test | Meniscus Tear
purpose: Childress's (1957) squat-walk test, designed for easily missed isolated lesions of the posterior third of the medial meniscus (vague onset, no synovial reaction, no true locking; patients often worked in a squatting position).
structure: Menisci, originally the posterior medial meniscus; in validation the test scored equally for anterior, posterior, medial and lateral tears.
procedure: SOURCE ISSUE: the page's execution paragraph is copied from the joint-line-tenderness page (supine palpation at 90° flexion) and does not describe the duck walk itself. The actual squat-walk execution is only shown in the video.
positive: Per the page text: reproduction of the patient's familiar pain (same wording as the joint-line-tenderness page).
notes: Clinical value rated rather weak because of limited accuracy. Other meniscus tests: McMurray, joint line tenderness, Ege's, Apley's, Finochietto, Thessaly.

title: Finochietto Test / Jump Sign | Meniscus Tear Assessment
purpose: Detect displacement of a torn posterior meniscal horn during a forceful anterior drawer in deep flexion.
structure: Posterior horn of the meniscus; incidence of meniscus tears about 61 per 100,000, one third sports-related; traumatic peripheral tears under 30 years, complex/degenerative patterns in older adults.
procedure: Knee flexed to 130-140° and fixated. The examiner pulls the tibia anteriorly as in the anterior drawer test but more aggressively.
positive: A palpable 'jump' as the torn posterior horn displaces anterior to the tibiofemoral contact point; barely audible or visible and not necessarily painful. Laxity from an ACL/PCL tear does not count; loose bodies or a discoid meniscus can also give a positive test.

accuracy.source: n/a: not validated by any diagnostic study (Shrier et al. 2010)

notes: Clinical value unknown. Shrier et al. 2010 argue that because meniscal tears are heterogeneous, test choice should follow which part of the meniscus each test stresses rather than pooled Sn/Sp. Other meniscus tests: McMurray, joint line tenderness, Ege's, Apley's, duck walk, Thessaly.
